extracted.intended_audience: experimental philosophers / natural philosophers (investigators of nature, early scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and interpreting experiments in natural philosophy: how to render imperceptible phenomena sensible, observe gradual processes, choose substitute instances, and measure space/time/quantity/predominance in natural powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to the sensible sphere
rubrics_metrics.description: All delicate experiments on natural or artificial bodies, by which the genuine are distinguished from the adulterated, and the better from the more common, should be referred to this division; for they bring that which is not the object of the senses within their sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use instruments and contrivances (e.g., thermometer, evaporation into a bladder) and artificial separations to render imperceptible natures perceptible; seek methods that bring invisible properties into the scope of the senses and pursue such experiments 'everywhere diligently'. Examples: weighing and evaporating spirits of wine to measure expansion, slow boiling of different liquids in glass to observe different modes of opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid introducing artefacts by the method (beware superinduced qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: In attacking bodies by fire, or other methods, many qualities are superinduced by the fire itself, and the other bodies used to effect the separation, which were not originally in the compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on violent heats or too energetic agents which destroy delicate conformations and create fallacies; recognize that some vapor or qualities observed (e.g., vapor from water by fire) may be produced by the experimental procedure rather than pre-existing in the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful experimental control and quantitative measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design experiments to control confounding factors and measure quantities precisely to determine the nature and degree of effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of good practice: use a small vessel to minimize heat required; note exact weight of liquid and vessel before and after; evacuate air from a bladder and seal with oil; prick bladder immediately after heating to prevent reconden­sation; compute volumes/expansions from measured weights and spaces. Other experimental illustrations: glass egg suction experiment, leaden globe compression and press to measure compressibility of water, bell-and-globe water experiment to study air compression/escape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use other animals' senses when human senses insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes reduction is not to human senses but to those of other animals whose senses exceed ours in certain respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ animals (dogs for scent, cats/owls for night vision) when they naturally perceive aspects (slight air-light, scents) that humans cannot; consider the sensory proportions of different species when choosing observational strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Itinerant/jointed instances (observe gradual motions/processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which indicate the gradually continued motions of nature; observe nature during her work rather than only finished products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch processes from their beginning through regular intervals to see progressive change (e.g., pull up seeds daily to study germination, observe hatching to see which parts form from yolk vs white); apply same continuous observation to inanimate processes (e.g., slow heating of water, wine, milk) to discern differences of behavior over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary/substitutive instances — substitution by approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution by approximation supplies information where senses are deficient, using materials/ media that comparatively deaden or alter effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a direct medium preventing an effect is unknown, compare how different media attenuate an action (e.g., magnet attracting iron through various materials); use comparative degrees (more or less) to approximate the behavior of the true inaccessible medium. Use when appropriate instances cannot be obtained but understand limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary/substitutive instances — substitution by analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution by analogy reduces imperceptible processes to perceptible ones by considering some similar perceptible body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogies cautiously (e.g., compare oil/water mixing to flame/air mixing, or quicksilver/dust/smoke behaviour as images of aëriform substances); first investigate whether the analogy is justified, since analogy is 'useful, but less sure.' Confirm analogical inferences with appropriate instances when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lancing/twitching instances (instances of Democritus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that 'twitch' or pierce the understanding by pointing out exquisite subtilty and amazing effects in nature, awakening attention to observation and inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select striking, small-scale phenomena to rouse curiosity and reveal subtle powers (examples: a drop of ink drawn into many letters, a little saffron coloring a tub of water, musk perfume diffusing widely, magnet attracting through bodies). Also note limits of such instances: dissimilar actions (different natures) may not impede each other, whereas similar ones can subdue one another (e.g., sun extinguishes candle light).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the rod or rule (measure by space/distance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which measure the powers and motions of bodies by space: determine the definite and limited spaces in which powers act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe whether powers act only in contact or at a distance, and establish the boundaries of action (dependent on mass, vigor, and medium). Examples and considerations: contact effects (touch, taste), near-distance magnetic attractions, long-distance effects (earth's magnetism, tides, rays of light), telescopes to extend perception; note also spherical expansion/contraction and limits of compressibility/extension (inflated bladder, leaden globe experiments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of the course (measure by time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which measure nature by moments of time; all motion and natural action take place in definite times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine absolute and relative durations and the timing of effects (e.g., orbital returns, tides, descent/ascent of bodies, rate of explosion sound vs light). Pay special attention to relative measures of motion (velocity differences produce different practical effects — e.g., gunpowder expansion outruns gravity) and to first/last in processes (first-extracted substances vs later ones in infusion/distillation). Use time-measurement to make practice effective and to explain phenomena such as apparent vs true time/place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances of quantity (doses of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that measure powers by the quantity of bodies and determine how quantity affects degree of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how effects vary with scale (some powers require large masses to appear, others act only in small quantities); do not assume simple proportionality (double quantity does not necessarily double effect). Determine exact proportions by experiment (examples: new wine and beer ripening in small skins vs large casks, herb infusion differences, magnet's attracting power relative to its size). Guard against over- or under-estimating requisite doses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrestling instances (instances of predominance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances that show predominance and submission of powers compared with each other — which is more energetic or inferior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study how motions and effects of bodies compound, decompose and combine to see which power predominates in interaction. Begin by cataloguing principal kinds of motions (e.g., resistance of matter, motion of connection) to compare comparative strength. Use such comparative experiments to determine which principles dominate in composite phenomena.
